‘What is the role of international environmental law in addressing environmental challenges? 
What are its most considerable limitations? Discuss using a specific environmental challenge of 
your choice’ 
 
 
LAWPP09 – Essay One 
 
Student Number: 3045050 
 
University of Stirling 
 
March 2022

Introduction 
The existence of international law (IL), let alone international environmental law (IEL), and its efficiency 
is a matter of discussion in literature1. Those who argue that IL does not exist point out the fact that 
there is not an enforcement mechanism to make sure that international rules are applied by countries. 
Another supporting fact in favour of this argument is that countries are considered to be sovereign units 
in the Westaphalian international system and cannot be forced to renounce their sovereign rights to 
another country or organisation. Therefore, international law can be realised to the extent of the 
countries’ willingness to do so. This argument, being correct in principle, must not lead to a thinking that 
all aspects of international law have evolved at a similar pace or that all of them suffer from the same 
level of inapplicability. Even though an understanding of a linear development of historical processes 
seems far from being a reality, and history includes backs and forwards in terms of evolution of laws, 
institutions, cultures etc., it is plausible to argue that IEL, though insufficient, has developed throughout 
the last two centuries and become one of the dominating agendas of the international community. This 
article specifically focuses on how climate change mitigation efforts have evolved within IEL, and the 
legal challenges affected by economic and political factors that lie as obstacles before the proliferation 
of these efforts within IEL. Therefore, the article begins with a brief analysis of the vulnerabilities of IEL, 
following the analysis of the UNCCC based primarily on a comparison and documentation of the Kyoto 
Protocol and Paris Climate Agreement and the criticisms directed against their composition. In 
conclusion, the study argues that shortcomings of international environmental cooperation do not have 
anything to do with the discipline of environmental law itself, which is created, aligned, or most often 
violated by states themselves. 
The role of International Law in addressing the environmental challenges 
 
ILE is not immune to the deficiencies of IL and can be considered one of its least improved aspects. For 
an area to be considered developed within IL, according to the orthodox view, the main sources of 
international law, which are treaties, customary law, and general principles of law2 can be expected to 
be well-grounded3. At this point the question regarding how to measure whether a rule is well-grounded 
comes at fore. As a response, it can be argued that whether an agreement has a non-binding or binding 
nature determines the reliability of that agreement. Therefore, how an agreement is worded is vital to 
understand the degree of its binding nature.  
Regarding the effectiveness of customary international law and general principles of law, case law can 
be a guide. When it comes to international environmental law, while it is seen that agreements in

cannot be underestimated. Moreover, transnational movements and actors such as non-governmental 
organisations have gradually gained influence on the development and enforcement of IEL through 
pressures on institutions for accountability4. Yet there are some obstacles as to enforceability of IEL 
which are political and economic in nature. 
Global South and North Division 
 
The international system is a combination of two factors which are the Westphalian nation-state system 
and, as an economic model, the global capitalist system. These factors provide the basis for the legal 
context of environmental issues and constitute the main challenges before tackling them. They do so for 
two reasons: 1) the nation-state system is based on the premise of sovereign units which cannot be 
forced to transfer their sovereign rights to another political entity, 2) global capitalist system is centered 
on the ambition of continues growth where natural resources -either biotic or abiotic- in states’ lands 
are considered to be national wealth, a premise that grants the sovereign states the right to exploit 
them freely unless otherwise is agreed on by law5. 
 
Blurred nature of concepts in international environmental law 
 
Some concepts in IEL such as environment and sustainable development or climate change do not have 
clear definitions. Regarding the concept of climate change, the developing scientific understanding of its 
nature has preceded its transposition into a legal plane throughout decades. On the other hand, 
codification of environmental issues does not simply correlate with the level of scientific awareness 
gained towards them. This said, while handling transboundary environmental issues, states do often 
have conflictual stands on a range of points from definitions of concepts to the determination of 
measures and responsibilities to mitigate them. Therefore, it can be argued that this ambiguity or 
disagreement on definitions is not solely due to an academic disagreement amongst states, but 
conversely, is political in nature as how those concepts are defined determines the way of sharing the 
burden amongst different stakeholders such as states, business sectors and international organisations. 
Therefore, gaining insight into the legal nature of the concepts regarding environmental issues is, while 
vital, hard to achieve. Regarding the term “environment,” Dupuy et al. offer three ways to understand 
whether it was attached legal effects: looking at 1) the founding instruments of IEL, 2) decisions of 
international courts and tribunals, 3) definition of the term within a specific normative context such as a

rather than “breach,” and “consequences” rather than “remedies” or “sanctions.”8

Climate Change Mitigation Efforts in International Environmental Law 
 
Climate change is a concept that includes global warming, and extreme weather events such as heat 
waves, heavy rains and so on9. This phenomenon is primarily a result of the greenhouse gas (GHG) 
emissions, or anthropogenic emissions, into the troposphere from the industrial revolution onward. 
There are two pillars of Climate Change regime: scientific pillar (IPCC) and policy pillar10. The reports of 
the scientific body have triggered political initiatives to tackle climate change since the 1990s onwards11. 
Two major difficulties in these political initiatives were defining the scope of UNFCCC and how to deal 
with the differences between developed and developing countries12. Regarding the first problem, the oil 
importing countries were pressing for a framework convention which does not entail countries to be 
bound with specific obligations, while the opposite camp was standing against a simply framed 
convention13. The second problem has been about how to share the burden of tackling climate change 
amongst countries14. Article 3 of the UNFCCC mentions the principles of the regime which are 
precautionary principle, principle of inter-generational equity, and the principle of common but 
differentiated responsibilities, while Article 4 distributes the responsibilities among parties in 
accordance with their level of development15. 
The Kyoto Protocol 
 
The Kyoto Protocol is considered to be a top-down approach to tackling climate change16. Dupuy et al. 
(2018) also argue that the following adoption of Berlin Mandate which focuses on committing 
obligations to the countries listed in Annex 1, protocols to UNFCCC has further deepened the gap of 
responsibilities amongst the parties making them obsolete in the end17. In case of the Kyoto Protocol, 
which required ratification of countries whose GHG emissions corresponded to 55% of total emissions of 
Annex 1 countries based on the year 1990, was born dead as the US disavowed the Protocol and Russia 
ratified it too late18. And emerging countries whose emissions were expected to increase were not 
subject to obligations under the Protocol19.

Trade of emissions 
 
Art. 17 of Kyoto Protocol grants the right to trade the emission allowance amongst countries. This 
mechanism, called Clean Development Mechanism (CDM), enables countries who wish to emit more 
than their allowance envisaged in the Protocol to buy emission allowance of other countries who emit 
less than their share20. Yet, this carbon market has been criticised as an invention of a new way to make 
profit, in other words accumulation of capital, within capitalist economic system without addressing the 
core issues that cause environmental degradation21. Moreover, the clean development projects in 
developing countries conducted under this mechanism to buy carbon credits have been criticised by 
creating a sub-imperialist inequality as most of these projects have been conducted in leading 
developing countries that are Brazil, China, and India while the whole continent Africa hosts only 1.86% 
of those projects22. Another challenge before the successful implementation of this mechanism is the 
tendency of private companies for commodifying certified emission reduction (CER) credits. This is done 
by companies who do not need CER credits but invest in clean development projects to acquire them 
and sell to other companies23. Böhm et al. (2018) argue that carbon market is a way of artificial 
commodification of a currently non-commodified entities, and therefore a way of expanding the 
frontiers of capitalist accumulation24. Therefore, the extent of this mechanism contributes to tackling 
climate change is a matter of discussion because of the economic understanding it is based on.  
 
The Paris Agreement on Climate Change 
 
 The Paris Agreement signed in 2015 was aimed to reverse this top-down approach to a bottom-up one, 
motivating the parties to adopt nationally determined contributions25 rather than obliging them to reach 
an agreed level of GHG reduction which in the example of the Kyoto Protocol proved unsuccessful. 
Rajamani (2016) argues that the Paris Agreement was worded in such a way that it was delicately 
calibrated, mixing provisions at two extremes with hard-obligations and non-obligations26.

The political will of countries to undergo international obligations for tackling climate change is a 
variable that determines the destiny of the international agreements on the subject. That was the 
reason of adoption the bottom-up approach at Paris Agreement which enabled the countries to 
contribute to climate change mitigation efforts through a nationally determined target, a flexibility 
which was thought to encourage the parties to come together and cooperate. This agreed solution was 
also a try to include the US to the Paris Agreement, whose Republican senators had opposed to undergo 
environmental commitment in international forum, and China who is the main emitter in the developing 
world27.  
The Paris Agreement has three elements that are goals, action areas and implementation techniques. 
The preambular paragraph 12 refers to human rights in a climate change agreement for the first time28. 
The Agreement represents a try to strike balance amongst parties who are hit by climate change 
directly, such as low-lying island states, and the others who are deemed not to be affected this 
severely29. Indeed, Ourbak & Magnan (2017) attribute Small Island Developing States (SIDS) the success 
of showing leadership in amplifying the ambitious goal of keeping global warming below 1.5 °C30, 
although such a goal was not recognised in the Paris Agreement. Article 2(2) of the Agreement refers to 
the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities while omitting the other two UNFCCC 
principles which are precaution and intergenerational equity31. Yet, Dupuy et al. (2018) interpret this as 
that climate change is no longer accepted as a matter of precaution, but rather an acknowledged risk 
that is to be prevented32. However, this does not provide an answer for the omission of the principle of 
intergenerational equity in the agreement even though it was stated in the preamble, which is accepted 
not to have a binding nature, while the term sustainable development (which includes intergenerational 
equity in its definition of Brundtland Report33) was referred to in the body of the agreement. This said, it 
is not surprising that intragenerational equity principle, which requires equity within a generation, was 
also not mentioned in the agreement. As an action area, mitigation is considered to be the soft belly of 
the agreement34 as it relies on the nationally determined contributions (NDCs) of countries35. Since the 
agreement adopted a bottom-up approach, the means to enforce the NDCs of countries are made up of 
soft-natured tools such as ”transparency and reporting, peer review, periodic stocktaking, public

Conclusion 
International environmental law is a growing body of sub-discipline under international law. Therefore, 
it suffers from the limitations of international law more than some other sub-disciplines of international 
law do. This is because of the conflictual nature of environmental issues on which the parties adopt 
different stand points in accordance with their economic, social, and political interests. However, this is 
not to claim that environmental law does not have a substantial effect on endorsing the initiatives for 
tackling environmental challenges. From the 1970s onwards, there has been a growing public interest in 
and pressure for accountability by NGOs about environmental issues which brought parties together to 
draw on the ways of tackling those issues. When it comes to climate change, it has been an area about 
which scientific certainty took time to gradually emerge and push for international cooperation. Even 
when scientific certainty became evident, the political and economic interests of states presented an 
obstacle before the adoption of mitigation measures on the international fora. The US’s disavowal of the 
Kyoto Protocol and Russian’s late accession resulted in failure of reaching the initially intended goals of 
reducing GHG emissions. The Protocol was interpreted as a top-down regulation creating binding 
obligations for the parties which were deemed to be the reason for the failure as they discouraged some 
countries to ratify the Protocol. The invention of the carbon market, while one of the seemingly working 
aspects of the Protocol, has been criticised for creating a new form of capitalist accumulation through 
commodification of certified emission reduction (CER) credits, therefore melting in the profit-induced 
logic of capitalist economy. The Paris Agreement, drawing on the failure of top-down enforcement of 
the Protocol, adopted a bottom-up approach with an ambition to motivate countries to cooperate for 
tackling climate change based on their nationally determined contributions. This time tools such as peer 
pressure and transparency were utilised as the means of enforcement which have not proved efficient 
in terms of achieving the goals set by the Agreement in so far. However, international environmental 
law cannot be held responsible for the failure of achieving the goals of international environmental 
agreements. Conversely, it is states who can and should define the scope of international environmental 
cooperation through codification of environmental responsibility and obligations and abiding by them. 
Pouncing on international environmental law, instead of states, for the failure of envisaged goals is 
similar to blaming a food for being tasteless rather than the incompetence of its cook.
